d3.overview: Domain III governs the build: planning and designing an AI system, assessing its impacts before committing, governing the data that feeds it, testing the resulting models, and taking the system through release into monitored operation. Its center of gravity is evidence — documented lifecycles, lineage, impact assessments, and test results that prove the system was built deliberately.
d3.exam: Roughly 21–25 questions. Expect deep scenario testing on data governance (lawful sourcing, quality, representativeness), the testing taxonomy (unit, integration, validation, performance, security, bias, adversarial), and impact assessments. Questions often hinge on sequencing — what must happen before training, before testing, before release.
key_points: Spans BOK subdomains III.A (design & building), III.B (training & testing data), and III.C (release & monitoring)
Documentation artifacts to know: model cards, datasheets, system cards, impact assessments, risk registers
Data governance pillars: lawful authority to use data, quality, representativeness, lineage/provenance, minimization, security
Testing must cover more than accuracy: robustness (edge cases), fairness (across groups), security (poisoning, inversion, adversarial examples), explainability
Overfitting/underfitting, drift, and representativeness failures are the recurring technical failure modes governance must catch

d4.overview: Domain IV governs deployment and use: evaluating whether and how to deploy (use-case fit, model type, deployment environment), running the key pre-deployment assessments (impact assessment of the selected system, vendor and licensing terms, proprietary-model risks), and then governing the operating system — policies, monitoring, audits, incidents, records, communications, and eventual retirement. The unifying idea is that governance does not end at launch — it intensifies.
d4.exam: Roughly 21–25 questions, and IV.C alone carries 9–11 of them. Scenarios dominate: choosing deployment options, vetting vendor terms, degraded accuracy discovered by monitoring, incidents requiring disclosure, systems needing rollback or retirement. The tested instinct is continuous verification — monitor, investigate root causes, document, remediate, communicate.
key_points: Spans BOK subdomains IV.A (deployment evaluation), IV.B (assessment activities), and IV.C (governing deployment & use)
IV.A weighs use-case context, model-type differences, and deployment options — including fine-tuning, RAG and agentic architectures — before anything ships
IV.B runs the due diligence: an impact assessment on the selected system, vendor and licensing terms, and the risks and opportunities of deploying a proprietary model
IV.C is the operating regime: policies, continuous monitoring, audits and red teaming, incident documentation, external communications, deactivation
The EU AI Act mandates post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting for high-risk systems

ch10.overview: BOK III.C — governing release, monitoring, and maintenance: pre-release readiness (model cards complete, conformity requirements met, stress and adversarial testing passed), controlled release strategies (canary, phased, shadow), and the continuous monitoring and maintenance regime that watches performance, drift, fairness, and security once real users and real data arrive.
ch10.exam: The heaviest Domain III subdomain at 8–10 questions. Deployment-strategy vocabulary is tested directly (canary vs. phased vs. shadow), and monitoring scenarios are a staple: accuracy degrades, drift is detected — the right answer investigates root causes and follows the escalation path, never 'keep running as-is.'
key_points: Pre-release readiness: model cards, conformity requirements, formal risk/impact reviews signed off before go-live
Release strategies manage blast radius: canary (small % first), phased rollout (expanding cohorts), shadow mode (parallel, non-authoritative), A/B
Data drift = input distribution shifts; concept drift = input→output relationship shifts; monitoring must catch both
Maintenance runs on a schedule: retraining windows, dependency patching, periodic performance/reliability/safety assessments
Public disclosures belong here too: technical documentation, deployment instructions, post-market monitoring evidence

ch11.overview: BOK IV.B — the key assessment activities that precede putting a chosen system into use: performing or reviewing an impact assessment on the selected system in its deployment context, evaluating the key terms and risks in the vendor or licensing agreement, and weighing the risks and opportunities unique to deploying a proprietary model — increased obligations and higher potential liability.
ch11.exam: 5–7 questions. Scenarios present an organization about to deploy a third-party, open-source or in-house model and ask what must be assessed first. Strong answers name the specific due-diligence set: an impact assessment on the actual system and use, and license and contract review — not generic 'do a risk assessment.' BOK v2.1 dropped the separate 'identify applicable laws' item; legal questions now sit in Domain II.
key_points: Impact assessments re-run against the SELECTED model in its real deployment context — a design-phase assessment of a different model doesn't transfer
Legal applicability still matters in practice, but v2.1 tests it through Domain II (II.A–II.C) rather than as an IV.B indicator
Vendor and open-source terms allocate risk: data-use rights, warranties, audit rights, update obligations, liability caps, license conditions
Proprietary-model deployment carries heightened obligations and liability — you answer for behavior you cannot fully inspect
Open-source is not obligation-free: license terms bind, and security/compliance burden shifts to the deployer

ch12.overview: BOK IV.C — governing AI in operation, the largest subdomain in the BOK: applying the operating policies (data governance, risk management, issue management, user training), continuous monitoring and maintenance, periodic assessments (audits, red teaming, threat modeling, security testing), documenting incidents and risks, forecasting secondary and unintended uses and downstream harms, running external communication plans, and executing deactivation and localization policies when regulation or performance demands it.
ch12.exam: The single heaviest subdomain on the exam at 9–11 questions. Incident lifecycle order, audit independence, records discipline, truthful external communication, and governed retirement are all reliable scenario territory. 'Fix quietly and move on' and 'one-time signoff' are the planted wrong answers.
key_points: Risk register discipline: owner, likelihood, impact, treatment, residual risk — the living record auditors ask for first
Audits need independence, defined criteria, evidence, and tracked remediation; red teaming and threat modeling recur periodically, not once
Incident lifecycle: detect → contain → investigate root cause → remediate → disclose as required → institutionalize lessons
Records prove governance happened: decisions, tests, approvals, incidents, versions — retained per schedule (EU AI Act: 10 years for high-risk providers)
Forecast secondary/unintended uses and downstream harms — deployment approval attaches to a use case, not to the model in general
External communications must be accurate (FTC §5 exposure) and planned in advance; deactivation/localization policies predefine the exit

ch13.overview: BOK IV.A — evaluating the factors that shape a deployment decision before any assessment or rollout begins: the use-case context (business objectives, required performance, data availability, ethical considerations, workforce readiness), the differences among AI model types (classic vs. generative, proprietary vs. open-source, small vs. large, language vs. multimodal), and the differences among deployment options (cloud vs. on-premises vs. edge; using a model as-is vs. fine-tuning vs. retrieval-augmented generation vs. agentic architectures).
ch13.exam: 6–8 questions. Expect trade-off scenarios: an organization with strict data-residency needs (→ on-prem/edge), a narrow task with tight latency budgets (→ smaller model), a knowledge-currency problem (→ RAG over retraining). The tested skill is matching the deployment configuration to the context, not naming the fanciest option.
key_points: Use-case factors first: business objectives, performance requirements, data availability, ethics, and workforce readiness gate everything downstream
Model-type axes: classic vs. generative, proprietary vs. open-source, small vs. large, language vs. multimodal — each axis trades capability against cost, control, and risk
Deployment environments: cloud (scale, third-party exposure), on-premises (control, cost), edge (latency, privacy, hard updates)
Adaptation spectrum: as-is (fastest, least fit), fine-tuning (domain fit, inherits base-model risk), RAG (current knowledge, injection surface)
Every choice here re-scopes the risk assessment — IV.A decisions are inputs to IV.B assessments

Agentic architectures (new in BOK v2.1) let the model plan and act through tools — risk scales with autonomy and action-space, so they need least-privilege permissions, approval checkpoints for high-stakes actions, and a kill switch

t_deployfactors.overview: The context questions that come before any model or vendor choice: what business objective does this deployment serve, what performance does the use case actually require, is the necessary data available and usable, what ethical considerations attach, and is the workforce ready — trained, resourced, and organizationally prepared — to operate it.
t_deployfactors.exam: Scenario stems often bury the deciding factor: a team with no ML operations experience (workforce readiness), a use case without accessible data (data availability), or objectives nobody quantified (business objectives). The correct answer addresses the missing factor before proceeding.
key_points: Business objectives make success measurable — without them, validation thresholds and monitoring targets have no anchor
Performance requirements are use-case-relative: triage support and playlist ranking demand different evidence
Data availability includes rights and quality, not just existence
Ethical considerations at evaluation stage are the cheap ones — declining a bad use case costs nothing downstream
Workforce readiness is a deployment risk: capable systems operated by unprepared teams produce incidents

t_modeltypes.overview: The model-type axes a deployment evaluation weighs: classic (discriminative, task-specific) versus generative models; proprietary versus open-source; small versus large; language-only versus multimodal. Each axis is a trade — capability against cost, vendor support against transparency, breadth against control — and the BOK expects governance professionals to reason about all four.
t_modeltypes.exam: Trade-off matching: strict auditability needs favor transparent/classic or open-source models; broad conversational capability favors large generative ones — with confabulation and content risks attached. No axis has a universally right end; context decides.
key_points: Classic/discriminative models predict within defined tasks; generative models create content and carry confabulation, IP, and content-safety risks
Proprietary: vendor support and frontier capability, but limited inspectability and contractual dependence
Open-source: transparency and control, but the deployer inherits security, hosting, and compliance burden — and license terms still bind
Small models: cheaper, faster, easier to govern; large models: broader capability, bigger risk surface and cost
Multimodality multiplies use cases and failure modes together — each modality adds its own bias and content risks

t_deployopts.overview: How and where the model runs: environment choices (cloud's managed scale versus on-premises control versus edge's local-inference latency and privacy), and adaptation choices (deploying a model as-is, fine-tuning it on domain data, or wrapping it in retrieval-augmented generation for grounded, current answers). These decisions shape performance, cost, data residency, and the entire monitoring architecture.
t_deployopts.exam: Configuration-matching scenarios: data-residency mandates point on-prem or edge; a need for current, citable knowledge without retraining points to RAG; domain-specific tone and vocabulary point to fine-tuning. Each choice's risk tail (RAG → indirect prompt injection; fine-tuning → inherited base-model risk) is the follow-up question.
key_points: Cloud: scalability and managed infrastructure, with third-party and data-residency exposure to assess
On-premises: maximum control and sovereignty at higher operational cost; edge: latency and privacy wins, update and monitoring logistics costs
As-is deployment is fastest but least fitted; validate against your population anyway
Fine-tuning buys domain fit and inherits the base model's biases, memorized data, and license constraints
RAG grounds outputs in retrieved sources — reducing confabulation, enabling citations, and opening the indirect-injection surface
Agentic architectures: the model calls tools and takes actions toward goals — weigh the gain against autonomy and action-space risk (see Agentic AI)

t_deployimpact.overview: The pre-deployment due diligence the BOK names first in IV.B: performing or reviewing an impact assessment on the actual selected system in its actual deployment context — because impacts are use-and-system-specific and do not transfer automatically from design-phase work or another deployment. (v2.0.1 also listed 'identify applicable laws' here; v2.1 removed it.)
t_deployimpact.exam: The trap is staleness: a scenario offers an impact assessment done on a different model, an earlier version, or a different use case — the correct answer re-assesses against what is actually being deployed. Applicable-law analysis follows the use, not the technology.
key_points: Impact assessments attach to a model-in-context: new model, new version, or new use case → new assessment
Legal context still shapes the assessment (hiring, credit, EU users), but v2.1 tests the law itself in Domain II
Deployment-stage assessment covers operational, ethical, legal, and reputational risk — wider than the design-phase technical view
Outputs feed the go/no-go gate: unresolved high findings block deployment, not paper over it

t_vendorterms.overview: The contractual and licensing layer of deployment assessment: vendor agreements that allocate data-use rights, warranties, audit rights, update and incident obligations, and liability; open-source licenses whose conditions (attribution, copyleft, use restrictions) bind even without a vendor; and the heightened obligations that come with proprietary models whose training data and behavior cannot be independently verified.
t_vendorterms.exam: Scenarios test whether terms were actually reviewed: an open-source model adopted without license review, a vendor contract with no bias warranty or audit right, a proprietary model whose claims were taken on faith. The correct answers demand AI-specific terms, not generic procurement paper.
key_points: Vendor agreements should secure: data-use limits, performance and bias warranties, model-change notification, incident SLAs, audit rights, exit portability
Open-source licenses bind: attribution, copyleft, and AI-specific use restrictions are enforceable conditions, not suggestions
Proprietary models mean deploying what you cannot inspect — compensate with contractual assurances and independent testing
Sub-tier terms flow through: your vendor's base-model and data licenses become your compliance problem
Terms review is a deployment gate, not a legal formality after the fact

term:Proprietary vs. Open-Source Models.deep_dive: The control-versus-support axis of model selection: proprietary buys vendor accountability, managed updates, and often frontier capability at the price of opacity and contractual dependence; open-source buys transparency, customization, and cost control at the price of inheriting the security, hosting, and compliance burden yourself. The BOK names this axis explicitly as a deployment-evaluation factor.
term:Proprietary vs. Open-Source Models.exam_tip: Neither end is 'safer' in general — auditability needs favor open-source, accountability-through-contract needs favor proprietary; context decides.

term:Small vs. Large Models.deep_dive: The capability-versus-cost axis: large models bring breadth and emergent capability with heavy inference cost, latency, and a wider risk surface; small models are cheap, fast, controllable — and sufficient for most narrow tasks. Right-sizing is a governance act: over-provisioned capability is unassessed risk.
term:Small vs. Large Models.exam_tip: 'Use the most capable model' is a distractor — fitness for the specific use case, not maximum capability, is the tested principle.

term:Language vs. Multimodal Models.deep_dive: The modality axis of model choice: language-only models process text; multimodal models add images, audio, or video — expanding use cases and simultaneously multiplying failure modes, since every added modality carries its own biases, content risks, and evaluation burden. Multimodal evaluation is genuinely harder: each input-output combination needs testing.
term:Language vs. Multimodal Models.exam_tip: Multimodality expands the risk surface with the capability — an answer adding modalities without adding evaluation scope is incomplete.

term:Cloud, On-Premises & Edge Deploymen.deep_dive: The environment decision behind every AI deployment: cloud offers elastic scale and managed operations while importing third-party and data-residency exposure; on-premises keeps data and control in-house at real operational cost; edge pushes inference onto local devices for latency and privacy wins, with harder update, monitoring, and security logistics. Regulatory constraints (localization, sectoral rules) often decide before economics do.
term:Cloud, On-Premises & Edge Deploymen.exam_tip: Data-residency or sovereignty requirements in a scenario point away from cloud — the environment choice is a compliance decision, not just an infrastructure one.

term:Proprietary Model Deployment Obliga.deep_dive: What changes when the model you deploy is someone else's black box: you carry deployment obligations and liability for behavior you cannot inspect, you depend on vendor claims you cannot independently verify, and your continuity hangs on their update and support commitments. The BOK flags this as its own IV.B assessment item — compensating controls are contractual (warranties, audit rights, SLAs) and empirical (independent testing).
term:Proprietary Model Deployment Obliga.exam_tip: Deploying proprietary AI heightens rather than reduces your obligations — 'the vendor is responsible' is the planted wrong answer.
